rv.q: L.B. Browne’s debut play Safe House is a gripping and tense state-of-the-nation drama that is one of the best plays of the year.
L.B. Browne's beautifully written, imaginative story is a fisheye view of consequences suffered by one family when radical, unchallenged certainty is imposed.

Regardless, Browne's skillful acceleration of the story and the four top-notch central performances create a gripping experience that's likely to leave you thankful for whatever healthy family relationships you might have.
L.B. Browne exhibits the vision, style and control of craft to be a potentially important playwright in the company of those others.
This is a play that will make you think about what truly does go on behind closed doors – including your own.

In Safe House, an affecting and intense play written by L.B. Browne and directed by Benjamin Viertel, familial tensions that have been as solid as physical structures finally take physical form when a crisis occurs.
What makes Safe House most compelling is the distinction it draws between protection and control.
Fortunately, there is a solid play beneath the pile, and a passionate cast brings it to life with energy, conviction, and heart.

The problem is that Browne’s drama, directed by Benjamin Viertel and produced by split/decision, is so packed with crises, secrets, politics, illness, trauma and family dysfunction that eventually the play begins collapsing under the weight of everything it wants us to carry.
It’s a superb drama, a microcosm of what’s happening in America today.

cn.t: L.B. Browne's gripping debut "Safe House" earns strong praise as a tense, timely state-of-the-nation drama. Critics laud its incendiary family dynamics and powerful performances from Marc Kudisch and Karen Ziemba in this intimate bunker setting.
